panels.title: CPU Usage
panels.description: CPU consumed by the MariaDB container, as a percentage of a single core (100% = one full core; can exceed 100% on multi-core hosts). Sustained highs usually mean expensive or unindexed queries, heavy write load, or lock contention. Correlate spikes with slow requests on the backend; if it sits near the host's core limit during normal use, tune queries/indexes or allocate more CPU. Brief spikes during migrations or batch jobs are usually fine.

panels.title: Memory
panels.description: MariaDB container memory over time. Working Set = active memory that cannot be reclaimed under pressure (this is what counts toward OOM limits); RSS = anonymous (non-file-backed) memory; Cache = reclaimable page cache. For a database the Working Set is dominated by the InnoDB buffer pool and connection buffers and is expected to plateau near a configured ceiling — a plateau is healthy, a Working Set that climbs without bound may indicate misconfigured buffers or a connection leak. Working Set approaching the container limit risks an OOM kill (see the OOM Events panel).

panels.title: Network I/O
panels.description: Rate of network traffic in/out of the MariaDB container (bytes/sec). Receive is inbound (queries and writes from the backend); Transmit is outbound (result sets returned). Use this to understand query/result patterns and spot anomalies — a sustained transmit spike may signal an unbounded query returning large result sets; flat-zero when the app should be active can indicate the backend lost its DB connection.

panels.title: Disk I/O
panels.description: Rate of bytes read from / written to disk by the MariaDB container (bytes/sec). This is often the most important panel for a database. Sustained reads suggest the working set does not fit in the InnoDB buffer pool (cache misses hitting disk) — consider raising innodb_buffer_pool_size or adding memory. Sustained writes come from commits, the redo log, and flushing; persistent write saturation bottlenecks query latency and points to faster storage or write-reduction. Correlate with CPU and backend request latency.

panels.title: Uptime
panels.description: Time since the MariaDB container last started. Red for the first minute, yellow up to 5 minutes, green after. An unexpectedly low value means the database recently restarted or crashed — every restart drops all connections and clears in-memory caches (cold buffer pool), so expect a temporary spike in disk reads afterward. Check the OOM Events panel and container logs to find why; a frequently-resetting uptime signals a crash loop.

panels.title: Memory (Working Set)
panels.description: Current active (non-reclaimable) memory used by MariaDB — the value that counts against the container's memory limit, dominated by the InnoDB buffer pool. Green below 1 GB, yellow above 1 GB, red above 2 GB. Adjust these thresholds to your configured buffer pool size and container limit. If it stays red near the container limit, raise the limit or lower innodb_buffer_pool_size; values close to the limit make an OOM kill likely.

panels.title: OOM Events (24 h)
panels.description: Count of out-of-memory kills in the last 24 hours. Green at 0, red at 1 or more. Any value > 0 means the kernel killed the database for exceeding its memory limit — a hard event that drops all connections and can interrupt in-flight transactions. If > 0, raise the container memory limit and/or lower innodb_buffer_pool_size and per-connection buffers, and check Uptime for the resulting restart. Recurring OOM kills point to an under-provisioned limit or over-configured buffers.
